## Environment Hacking

<br>

Here I will demonstrate one possible way of signaling a 'random' random seed, and why it isn't enough to prevent seed hacking. Let's try using `Sys.time()`, and let's be extra generous and assume that a disinterested third party decided when to run this code, so that the seed produced by `Sys.time()` could not have been known by the author of the code (who wants to hack the results with a specific seed). Like the other examples in this repository, let's even assume this code was run automatically and transparently via a GitHub action[^1] in a way that anyone can audit and verify. Sounds like a pretty foolproof system, right? Not quite...
<br>

```{r, echo=FALSE}
box::use(dplyr[...])

## This is what's being 'injected' into the environment by Rscript -e "..."
# set.seed <- function(s){
#     base::set.seed(42)
# }

coin_flip <- function(n){
    res = sample(c(1,0), size=n, replace=TRUE)
    return(res)
}

read_data_transparently_published_on_osf <- function(identifier){
    project = osfr::osf_retrieve_node(paste0("https://osf.io/", identifier
    ,"/")) |> osfr::osf_ls_files()
    data_summary = osfr::osf_download(project, conflict="skip")
    df = read.csv(data_summary[["local_path"]]) 
    return(df)
}
```

```{r}
set.seed(Sys.time())
data = read_data_transparently_published_on_osf("dw2rz")

# 'preprocess' the data (really just an excuse to call the poisoned 
# dplyr::mutate function)
data = data |> dplyr::mutate(male = if_else(sex=="male", 1,0))

random_state_after_mutate = .Random.seed  # Saving for later demonstration

predictions = coin_flip(nrow(data))

cat("Accuracy: ", mean(predictions == data$male), "\n")
```


<br>
Despite setting a seed that was supposedly unknowable beforehand (`Sys.time()`), the accuracy of our coin flip model (which should be 50% at best) is over 97%! This is because the pre-selected seed that performs best (`42`) was secretly set by `dplyr::mutate`. However, when we look for any altered code in `dplyr::mutate`, we won't find any. 
<br>

```{r}
dplyr::mutate
```
<br>
The source code of `mutate` is pretty underwhelming, since it delegates functionality through the `UseMethod` function. If you trace the sequence of function calls that `mutate` kicks off, you'll eventually find a `.Call` function which calls `dplyr_mask_eval_all_mutate`, which has a signature that looks something like this:
<br>

```{cpp, eval=FALSE}
// dplyr/src/mutate.cpp  (C++ code) 
SEXP dplyr_mask_eval_all_mutate(SEXP quo, SEXP env_private) {
    ...
}
```
<br>
All I did was add some code inside this function that changes R's seed to `42` (which I will not show here but can easily be learned by anyone motivated enough to think about this kind of deception to begin with). 
<br>

```{r}
# Demonstrating that the random_state saved right after calling dplyr::mutate
# is the same as when you set.seed(42)
set.seed(42)

random_state_42 = .Random.seed

print(identical(random_state_after_mutate, random_state_42))
```

<br>
After the C++ code is compiled, it is very difficult to catch this deception, since the source code can be re-edited to appear as if nothing was changed. Indeed, this is what I did; you can find the source code that I used to install a local, edited version of dplyr in same GitHub [repository](https://github.com/cnsodano/BEACR-DEMO-Paul-Meehl-Grad-School-Meta-Research-Symposium) of this .Rmd file at `/dplyr/`.
